Creating Mocks with Jest →

What Is a Mock?

A fake stand-in for a real dependency, that lets a test control and inspect one collaborator without needing the real thing.

Lesson 1's unit test for ticket.service.js (Figure 1.14) worked by calling the real functions directly — there was nothing to fake, because the "database" underneath was just a plain array, already isolated and instant. That stops being true the moment those same functions talk to Prisma and a real MySQL server: calling them for real now means a network round trip, a database that has to already contain the right rows, and a test that quietly breaks the moment someone else's test changes what's in that database.

A mock solves this by standing in for a real dependency with a fake version you control completely. Instead of a real PrismaClient actually querying MySQL, a test can hand ticket.service.js an object that merely looks like one — same method names, but each one instantly returns whatever fixed value the test tells it to, no database involved at all. This is what makes it a unit test in the sense from Lesson 1's why-automated-testing topic: ticket.service.js is still being tested in isolation, one layer at a time — it's just that "isolation" now means isolating it from Prisma specifically, not from nothing.

A mock gives you two things a real dependency can't, on demand: control (you decide exactly what findUnique returns for this one test, without needing a real matching row anywhere) and inspection (you can ask afterward "was create actually called, and with what arguments?" — the next slide shows Jest's tools for exactly that).
